title: Siyagh al-Mubalagha (the Intensive Patterns of the Active Participle)

sections.text: Siyagh al-Mubalagha (the Intensive Patterns)

The intensive patterns (siyagh al-mubalagha) are derived nouns converted from the active participle into particular patterns, in order to denote the doer of an action together with abundance and intensity in that action. They convey what the active participle conveys, and add to it the sense of doing it much.

items.text: — The man forgives his companion's slip.
— Allah forgives the sins of those who repent, again and again.
— The student memorises his lesson.
— The student memorises all his lessons thoroughly.

sections.text: Look at the underlined words. 'Ghafir' and 'hafiz' are active participles on the pattern 'faʿil', denoting merely that the action occurred from the doer. 'Ghaffar' and 'hafiz (faʿil)' have been converted from the active participle into two other patterns so as to denote abundance and intensity. The basic meaning is one and the same; the difference lies in the measure of the action and how much of it there is.
What exactly is the difference between the active participle and the intensive pattern, if the meaning is the same?

The active participle denotes that the action occurred from its doer, with no regard to little or much: 'sadiq' is one from whom truthfulness occurred. The intensive pattern denotes that the action occurred from him abundantly, or powerfully, or habitually: 'saduq' and 'siddiq' denote one whose truthfulness became so frequent that it turned into his very character. That is why these patterns were chosen for the Beautiful Names of Allah: al-Ghaffar, al-Razzaq, al-Ghafur, al-Samiʿ, al-ʿAlim.
First: Conditions for Forming an Intensive Pattern

Intensive patterns are formed by rule (qiyas) from a triliteral verb that is fully inflecting, complete, and in the active voice; and it is most often transitive, so that the derived form can do the work of its verb and put a direct object in the accusative.

items: The verb must be triliteral: kataba → kattab; ʿalima → ʿallam. If it is not triliteral, forming an intensive from it is a matter of transmission, not rule.
It must be fully inflecting: no intensive is formed from frozen verbs such as 'laysa', 'ʿasa', 'niʿma', and 'biʾsa'.
It must be complete: no intensive is formed from the defective (copular) verbs such as 'kana', 'asbaha', and 'zalla'.
It must be in the active voice: no intensive is formed from a passive verb.
It is most often transitive; yet intensives have been formed from intransitive verbs as transmitted usage: nama → naʾum; sama → sawwam; qama → qawwam.
ghafara, ghaffar (he forgave — ever-forgiving)
ʿalima, ʿallam (he knew — all-knowing)
shakara, shakur (he thanked — deeply grateful)
samiʿa, samiʿ (he heard — all-hearing)
hadhira, hadhir (he was wary — ever-wary)

sections.text: Second: The Five Well-Known Patterns

The intensive patterns are many; the five best known and most frequent are: faʿʿal, mifʿal, faʿul, faʿil, and faʿil (the short one). They rank in intensity — and in how readily they govern — in that order.

headers: The verb it is taken from

sections.text: 1 — The Pattern 'Faʿʿal'

items: ghafara, ghaffar (he forgave — ever-forgiving)
razaqa, razzaq (he provided — ever-providing)
qatala, qattal (he killed — a great slayer)
taba, tawwab (he turned in mercy — ever-relenting)
masha, mashshaʾ (he walked — one who goes about much)

items.text: — Allah is ever-forgiving to whoever repents.
— My grandfather used to give his wealth away freely to the poor.

sections.text: 2 — The Pattern 'Mifʿal'

items: aʿta, miʿtaʾ (he gave — most generous)
aʿana, miʿwan (he helped — ever-helpful)
nahara, minhar (he slaughtered — one who slaughters much)
hadhara, mihdhar (he prattled — a great babbler)

items.text: — The generous man gives lavishly to those who ask.
— Do not be a babbler in your gathering.

sections.text: 3 — The Pattern 'Faʿul'

items: shakara, shakur (he thanked — deeply grateful)
sabara, sabur (he endured — greatly patient)
ghafara, ghafur (he forgave — most forgiving)
akala, akul (he ate — a great eater)
jahila, jahul (he was ignorant — deeply ignorant)

items.text: — The believer is greatly patient in affliction.
— Be deeply grateful for your Lord's blessing.

sections.text: When 'faʿul' carries the sense of the active participle, the masculine and the feminine are identical: you say 'rajulun sabur' (a patient man) and 'imraʾatun sabur' (a patient woman) — never 'saburatun'. But when 'faʿul' carries the sense of the passive participle it does take the taʾ: 'naqatun halubatun' (a milch camel), 'shatun rakubatun' (a riding ewe).
4 — The Pattern 'Faʿil'

items: samiʿa, samiʿ (he heard — all-hearing)
ʿalima, ʿalim (he knew — all-knowing)
qadara, qadir (he had power — all-powerful)
rahima, rahim (he had mercy — most merciful)
hafiza, hafiz (he guarded — ever-guarding)

items.text: — Allah hears the supplication of His servants.
— The believer keeps close guard over his tongue.

sections.text: 5 — The Pattern 'Faʿil' (Short)

items: hadhira, hadhir (he was wary — ever-wary)
fatina, fatin (he was shrewd — very shrewd)
yaqiza, yaqiz (he was alert — wide awake)
khashuna, khashin (he was rough — very rough)

items.text: — The soldier is ever on his guard against his enemy.
— Be shrewd about what is being plotted for you.

sections.text: The patterns that most readily govern are 'faʿʿal', 'mifʿal', and 'faʿul'; then 'faʿil'; and the least of them is the short 'faʿil'. The reason is that the strength of the resemblance to the active participle weakens the further the pattern moves from its shape.
Third: Other Patterns Known by Transmission
Other intensive patterns have come down from the Arabs. They are matters of transmission, not of rule: nothing new is formed on their model — only what has actually been transmitted is memorised.

rows: Rare transmitted usage; not found in the Qurʾan

items: humaza (a persistent slanderer)
lumaza (a persistent backbiter)
kubbar (enormous)
siddiq (utterly truthful)
sikkir (a habitual drunkard)
miʿtir (much-perfumed)

sections.text: Fourth: Intensive Patterns from Non-Triliteral Verbs

The default is that intensive patterns are formed only from triliteral verbs. Whatever has come from a non-triliteral verb is heard from the Arabs: it is memorised, and nothing is formed on its model.

items: aʿta, miʿtaʾ (he gave — most generous)
aʿana, miʿwan (he helped — ever-helpful)
aqdama, miqdam (he advanced — very bold)
adraka, darrak (he overtook — quick to grasp)
andhara, nadhir (he warned — a warner)
bashshara, bashir (he gave glad tidings — a bearer of good news)

sections.text: 'Miʿtaʾ' comes from the quadriliteral 'aʿta', 'darrak' from 'adraka', and 'nadhir' from 'andhara'. By rule these should have been 'muʿtin', 'mudrik', and 'mundhir' — the active-participle form of the non-triliteral verb. The rule was departed from in favour of the intensive as transmitted usage, not as a regular pattern.
Fifth: How the Intensive Pattern Governs

The intensive pattern does the work of its verb exactly as the active participle does: it puts a subject in the nominative, and a direct object in the accusative if its verb is transitive. The condition for its governing differs according to whether it carries the definite article 'al' or is stripped of it.
1 — Carrying the Article 'Al'

When the intensive pattern carries 'al', it governs unconditionally: no particular tense is required of it, and no support word is required before it — because the 'al' here is a relative particle meaning 'the one who'.

items.text: — I loved the man who freely gives his wealth to the poor.
— The one deeply grateful to his Lord came.

sections.text: In the first example 'al-wahhab' is an intensive pattern functioning as an adjective in the accusative; its subject is a hidden pronoun understood as 'huwa', and 'mala-hu' is its direct object in the accusative. In the second, 'al-shakur' is the subject of the verb, in the nominative; its own hidden subject refers back to it, and 'rabba-hu' is its direct object in the accusative. Neither one needed any further condition, because both carry 'al'.
2 — Stripped of 'Al'
When the intensive pattern is stripped of 'al' it governs only under two conditions together: it must denote the present or the future, not the past; and it must rest on a support word before it.

items: Preceded by an interrogative: a-qattal-un akhu-ka al-aʿdaʾ? (Is your brother a great slayer of enemies?)
Preceded by a negative: ma nassar-un Muhammad-un al-zalim (Muhammad is no great supporter of the wrongdoer).
Preceded by a vocative: ya miʿtaʾ-an al-fuqaraʾ, la-ka ajru-ka (O you who give lavishly to the poor, yours is your reward).
Falling as a predicate, thus resting on the subject: al-muʾmin-u hafiz-un lisana-h (The believer keeps close guard over his tongue).
Falling as an adjective, thus resting on the described noun: raʾaytu rajul-an hammal-an al-athqal (I saw a man who carries heavy loads).
Falling as a circumstantial accusative, thus resting on its subject: aqbala al-rajul-u shakur-an rabba-h (The man came forward, deeply grateful to his Lord).

items.text: — Is your brother a great slayer of enemies?
— Muhammad is no great supporter of the wrongdoer.
— The believer keeps close guard over his tongue.

sections.text: In 'a-qattalun akhuka al-aʿdaʾ?' the word 'qattal' rests on the interrogative hamza, so it is the subject of the nominal sentence, 'akhuka' is its own subject standing in place of the predicate, and 'al-aʿdaʾ' is its direct object. In 'ma nassarun Muhammadun al-zalim' it rests on the negative, and the parsing is the same. In 'al-muʾminu hafizun lisanah' it rests on the subject of the nominal sentence because it falls as the predicate; its own subject is a hidden pronoun understood as 'huwa', and 'lisanahu' is its direct object.

When an intensive pattern is formed from an intransitive verb — such as 'sabur' from 'sabara ʿala' and 'naʾum' from 'nama' — it puts a subject in the nominative but takes no direct object in the accusative, because its verb is not transitive by itself but only through a preposition.
Sixth: Telling the Active Participle, the Intensive Pattern, and the Resembling Adjective Apart

rows: faʿil from the triliteral; mufʿil and the like from others
The action occurring from its doer, as something arising and renewed
The action occurring from him with abundance and intensity
A fixed, permanent quality of its bearer, from an intransitive verb

sections.text: The patterns 'faʿil' and the short 'faʿil' are shared between the intensive pattern and the resembling adjective. The distinction lies in the underlying verb and its sense: if the verb is transitive and the description denotes something arising and renewed, it is an intensive pattern — like 'ʿalim' from 'ʿalima'. If the verb is intransitive and the description denotes something fixed and lasting, it is a resembling adjective — like 'karim' from 'karuma'.

items: ʿalim — an intensive pattern from the transitive 'ʿalima'
karim — a resembling adjective from the intransitive 'karuma'
hafiz — an intensive pattern from the transitive 'hafiza'
sharif — a resembling adjective from the intransitive 'sharufa'
hadhir — an intensive pattern from the transitive 'hadhira'
farih — a resembling adjective from the intransitive 'fariha'

sections.text: What is gained by turning from the active participle to the intensive pattern?

Both concision and emphasis. Instead of saying 'a man who forgives much and forgives often', you say 'a ghaffar of a man' and gather the whole meaning into a single word. That is why these patterns were chosen for praise and for blame alike: in praise, 'ghaffar', 'razzaq', 'wahhab'; in blame, 'humaza', 'lumaza', 'akul', 'mihdhar'.

sections.text: Do not confuse the intensive pattern with forms that share its shape but not its sense. The pattern 'mifʿal' also serves as a noun of instrument — miftah (key), minshar (saw), mizan (scale) — with no intensity in it at all. And the pattern 'faʿʿal' also denotes trades and crafts — najjar (carpenter), haddad (blacksmith), khabbaz (baker) — which is a noun for the trade, not an intensive. What decides the matter is the intended meaning, not the shape of the pattern.
A Worked Example

items.text: — Allah forgives, again and again, the sin of the one who repents.

sections.text: Iʿrab: 'Allahu' — the divine name, subject of the nominal sentence in the nominative, its marker the visible damma. 'Ghaffarun' — the predicate in the nominative, its marker the visible damma; it is an intensive pattern on the pattern 'faʿʿal' which does the work of its verb because it rests on the subject of the nominal sentence, and its own subject is a hidden pronoun understood as 'huwa'. 'Dhanba' — the direct object of the intensive pattern, in the accusative, its marker the visible fatha, and it is the first term of a construct. 'Al-taʾibi' — the second term of the construct, in the genitive, its marker the visible kasra.
Allah the Exalted said: "Indeed your Lord is the doer of whatever He wills." (Hud 11:107)

In this noble verse 'faʿʿalun' is an intensive pattern on the pattern 'faʿʿal' from 'faʿala'. It is the predicate of 'inna', in the nominative, its marker the visible damma. It conveys an intensity that the active participle 'faʿil' could not convey, and so it denotes the perfection of His power and the effectiveness of His will in whatever He wills, glory be to Him.
And Allah the Exalted said: "And He is the Ever-Forgiving, the Most Loving." (Al-Buruj 85:14)

'Al-ghafur' and 'al-wadud' are two intensive patterns on the pattern 'faʿul', and each is a predicate in the nominative. Notice that 'faʿul' here carries the sense of the active participle, so it took no taʾ — exactly as laid down in the rule above.
And Allah the Exalted said: "Woe to every scorner and mocker." (Al-Humaza 104:1)

'Humaza' and 'lumaza' are two intensive patterns on the transmitted pattern 'fuʿala': the first from 'hamaza', to find fault with someone to their face; the second from 'lamaza', to find fault behind their back. Both are in the genitive by annexation. In them is proof that the intensive patterns are used for blame just as they are used for praise.
And Allah the Exalted said: "Indeed he was a man of utter truth, a prophet." (Maryam 19:41)

'Siddiqan' is an intensive pattern on the transmitted pattern 'fiʿʿil' from 'sadaqa'. It is the predicate of 'kana', in the accusative, its marker the visible fatha. It is more emphatic than 'sadiq' and 'saduq' together, for it denotes one who reached the utmost in truthfulness until it never left him.
